issues.title: HIP-583 Alias on all transactions
issues.body:
### Problem

The first phase of [HIP-583](https://hips.hedera.com/hip/hip-583) Auto Account Creation added alias to crypto transfer transactions only. In the next phase, alias will be added to all transactions that take an `AccountID` as input.

### Solution

* Replace any uses of `EntityId.of(AccountID|ContractID)` that pulled from `TransactionBody` or `TransactionRecord` with `EntityIdService.lookup(AccountID|ContractID)`
* Deprecate `EntityId.of(AccountID|ContractID)` as we want to ensure the service is used going forward and also because we want to remove protobuf dependencies from common module. Or possibly don't deprecate if there remain a lot of uses not addressed by step one.

### Alternatives

_No response_

issues.title: Adversarial test suite: forged receipts must fail verification
issues.body:
**Level: intermediate · testing/security.** No new features — this hardens the repo's core promise. You need to understand what each receipt panel claims and how its verifier checks it; everything runs offline.

## Why

The pitch is "every panel independently verifiable." The positive path is proven by the demo; the **negative space** is not yet systematically proven: a forged or tampered receipt must fail verification, every time, for every panel. A mutation suite is the strongest evidence the stamps mean something.

## Where to look

Each panel has a verifier to attack:

- **Settlement** — [`src/verify.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/verify.ts) (`verifySettlement`, `toVerdict`): the `match` judgment against mirror rows.
- **Delivered content** — [`src/content.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/content.ts): sha-256 of the exact bytes, signed, signer key mirror-checked.
- **Consent** — the wallet-signed one-time challenge, re-verified against the approver's on-chain key (see the hub's wallet-approval mode and [`src/attestation.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/attestation.ts)).
- **Block proof** — [`src/stream.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/stream.ts): merkle root recomputed, threshold signature verified (`npm run provenance` path).

Tests live in `test/` (vitest); mirror responses are injectable via `fetchImpl`, the block source via `BlockSource` — no network needed.

## What to do

Build a tamper matrix: for each panel, enumerate single-field mutations and assert the verifier rejects (or downgrades) every one. Minimum set:

| Panel | Mutations that must fail |
| --- | --- |
| Settlement | amount off by **one tinybar** (over and under) · wrong recipient · wrong transaction id · mirror row for a different transfer |
| Content | one flipped byte in the body (hash mismatch) · valid hash, wrong signer key · valid signer, signature over different bytes

issues.title: Hub: show a running spend total against the cap
issues.body:
**Level: beginner · good first issue.** Front-end only — one file, no library changes, no funded accounts needed to develop (run the demo in mock mode).

## Why

The hub's human gate shows the terms of the *next* payment, and a **max spend** cap filters quotes — but there's no running total. A human approving the fifth request of a session has no on-screen answer to "how much has this agent already spent?" Adding a cumulative display makes the consent decision informed, not just per-transaction.

## Where to look

Everything is in [`demo/hub.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/demo/hub.ts) — the hub is a single self-contained page:

- The cap input is `#max-payment` (~line 640), denominated in the chosen asset (`data-asset`, `data-decimals` on the picker — the label already switches between ℏ and USDC, ~line 600).
- The run stream narrates each settlement (the `charged: quoted … → settled …` line) — that's where the settled amount and asset are available to accumulate.

## What to do

1. Accumulate settled amounts client-side as runs complete, **per asset** — an ℏ total and a USDC total must never be summed into one number (they're different units; keep them as separate atomic-unit tallies, formatted with each asset's decimals).
2. Display "spent this session" near the max-spend control; when a cap is set for the currently selected asset, show it as `spent / cap`.
3. Reset the tally on page reload is fine (session = page session); say so in the UI label.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Running total visible on the hub, updating after each settled run
- [ ] Per-asset tallies — switching the pay-for picker shows the matching asset's total
- [ ] Refused/declined runs add nothing (nothing was signed, nothing was spent)
- [ ] `npm run verify` passes (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md))

Nice-to-have, not required: a small warning style when the session total plus the next quote would exceed t

issues.title: Receipt JSON export alongside HTML
issues.body:
**Level: beginner · good first issue.** Self-contained, no network or funded accounts needed — the whole task runs offline against existing test fixtures.

## Why

Every paid run writes `receipt.html` — great for humans, opaque for machines. Agents that make many paid requests need to store, index, and re-verify receipts programmatically. A JSON export with a stable schema makes the receipt a data artifact, not just a page.

## Where to look

- [`src/receipt.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/receipt.ts) — `settlementReceiptHTML(...)` builds the HTML from a `SettlementVerdict` plus `ReceiptOptions` (delivered content, consent, proof panels). The JSON export consumes the **same inputs**; no new data is gathered.
- [`src/verify.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/verify.ts) — `SettlementVerdict` (fulfilment, request, receipts, transactionId, hashscanUrl, mirrorUrl) is most of the payload already.
- [`src/index.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/index.ts) — the public barrel; export the new function here.
- `test/` — see how the existing receipt tests build a verdict fixture; reuse it.

## What to do

1. Add `settlementReceiptJSON(verdict, options)` next to `settlementReceiptHTML`, returning a plain serializable object (not a string) with the same panels: settlement, delivered content, consent, proof — each carrying its trust stamp exactly as the HTML does (`UNVERIFIED` / `SERVER COMMITTED` / `VERIFIED` are claims, so they must survive the format change unchanged).
2. Include a top-level `schemaVersion: 1` so the format can evolve.
3. Export it from `src/index.ts`.
4. Document the schema in `docs/receipt-schema.md` (field-by-field, one line each).
5. Optionally: have the demo agent ([`demo/agent.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/demo/agent.ts)) write `receipt.json` beside `receipt.html`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `settlementReceiptJSON` exported from the bar

issues.title: Support any HTS token beyond testnet USDC and HBAR
issues.body:
**Level: advanced.** Cross-cutting design work: the quote scheme, the verifier, the spend policy, the receipt, and the hub all touch asset identity. Worth a short design comment in this thread before code.

## Why

The pay-for picker offers HBAR and testnet USDC today. The scheme already generalizes — asset `0.0.0` means HBAR in tinybars, anything else is an HTS token id in its smallest unit ([`src/requirements.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/src/requirements.ts)) — but the demo and several safety checks are specialized to the two known assets. Generalizing to *any* HTS token makes the repo a template for real paid APIs, not a two-asset demo.

## Where it touches

- **Quote side** — [`demo/server.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/demo/server.ts) / [`demo/shared.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/demo/shared.ts): a config surface for the server to advertise accepted assets (token id, decimals, display symbol) instead of the hardcoded pair.
- **Decimals** — currently known a priori (8 for ℏ, 6 for USDC). For arbitrary tokens, decimals must come from the mirror (`/api/v1/tokens/{id}`) and be treated as **verification input, not display trivia**: an amount judged with the wrong decimals is exactly the off-by-10^n bug the exact-amount guarantee exists to prevent.
- **Association** — the recipient (and the agent, for change/refund paths) must be associated with the token; auto-association may or may not cover it. Decide: pre-flight check with a clear refusal, vs. letting settlement fail and reporting honestly.
- **Spend cap** — [`demo/policy.ts`](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-x402/blob/main/demo/policy.ts) + the hub's cap input: the cap is denominated in the quote's asset. With N assets, per-asset caps (the current model, generalized) are simpler and more honest than any cross-asset conversion — recommend keeping caps strictly per-asset and refusing quotes in assets with no cap configured

issues.title: Add parameterized type to SchemaRegistry in Service interface
issues.body:
## Summary

The `Service` interface should use `SchemaRegistry<SemanticVersion>` instead of raw `SchemaRegistry` type to provide type safety when registering schemas.

## Current Situation

Currently, the `Service` interface uses a raw `SchemaRegistry` type:

```java
public interface Service {
    /**
     * Registers the schemas this application state really uses with the given {@link SchemaRegistry}.
     *
     * @param registry the registry to register the schemas with
     */
    void registerSchemas(@NonNull SchemaRegistry registry);
}
```

However, `SchemaRegistry` is a generic type that should be parameterized with a version type:

```java
public interface SchemaRegistry<V> {
    SchemaRegistry<V> register(@NonNull Schema<V> schema);
}
```

Using the raw type creates a type safety issue where there's no compile-time verification that schemas being registered match the expected version type.

## Proposed Solution

Change the `Service` interface to use the parameterized type:

```java
public interface Service {
    /**
     * Registers the schemas this application state really uses with the given {@link SchemaRegistry}.
     *
     * @param registry the registry to register the schemas with
     */
    void registerSchemas(@NonNull SchemaRegistry<SemanticVersion> registry);
}
```

## Benefits

1. **Type Safety**: Compile-time verification that all schemas use `SemanticVersion`
2. **Better IDE Support**: Auto-completion and type inference work correctly
3. **Consistency**: All Hedera services use `SemanticVersion` for schema versioning
4. **Catches Errors Early**: Prevents accidentally using wrong version type

## Related Code

- `Service` interface: `platform-sdk/swirlds-state-api/src/main/java/com/swirlds/state/lifecycle/Service.java` (line 43)
- `SchemaRegistry` interface: `platform-sdk/swirlds-state-api/src/main/java/com/swirlds/state/lifecycle/SchemaRegistry.java`
- `SemanticVersion`: `hapi/hedera-protobufs/services/basic_types.proto`

## Migration Notes

**Current implementation:**
```python
@classmethod
def _from_protobuf(cls, transaction_body):
    """
    Creates a transaction instance from protobuf components.

    This is an internal method that should be overridden by subclasses to restore
    transaction-specific fields.

    Args:
        transaction_body: The parsed TransactionBody protobuf
        body_bytes (bytes): The raw bytes of the transaction body
        sig_map: The SignatureMap protobuf containing signatures

    Returns:
        Transaction: A new transaction instance with all fields restored
    """
    transaction = cls()
```


### 💡 Solution

Update the docstring to accurately reflect the method signature and its purpose. Remove references to parameters that are not accepted by the method and ensure the return description matches the actual implementation.

issues.title: Bug: Assignment bots should refetch issue state before final assignment decision
issues.body:
## Description


The GFI and beginner `/assign` bots appear to use `context.payload.issue` from the original `issue_comment.created` webhook payload for the final assignment checks.

Because the webhook payload is a snapshot, a queued workflow run may not reflect issue state changes made by an earlier workflow run. For example, a later `/assign` run may still see `payload.issue.assignees` as empty even if the issue has already been assigned by the time that run executes.

This means the assignment decision may be based on stale issue state rather than the latest GitHub issue state.

## Files containing the relevant logic

- `.github/scripts/bot-gfi-assign-on-comment.js`
- `.github/scripts/bot-beginner-assign-on-comment.js`

Related workflows:

- `.github/workflows/bot-gfi-assign-on-comment.yml`
- `.github/workflows/bot-beginner-assign-on-comment.yml`

## Expected behavior

Before making the final assignment decision, the bot should verify the current issue state from the GitHub API, especially:

- current assignees
- current labels
- current issue state

If the issue is already assigned, the bot should not call `addAssignees`.

## Actual behavior

The current scripts appear to check `issue.assignees` from the webhook payload before calling `github.rest.issues.addAssignees(...)`.

In a close timing assignment scenario, this could lead to duplicate assignment attempts or follow-up automation running from stale assumptions.

## Why is this important

Both workflows use concurrency, which helps serialize workflow execution. However, concurrency does not refresh the original webhook payload.

So a later queued job can run after an earlier job has assigned the issue, while still seeing the original payload state:

```js
context.payload.issue.assignees = []
```
Refetching the issue before the final assignment decision would make the assignment bots safer against stale event data.

### Live timing scenario

1. Create or use an unassigned issue labeled

issues.title: Release workflow should create a GitHub Release on tag push
issues.body:
## Problem

Pushing a release tag (`v*.*.*`) triggers the [Release workflow](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-streams-rs/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml), which publishes the crate to crates.io and the Node binding to GitHub Packages — but nothing creates a GitHub Release. Tags only show up under [/tags](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-streams-rs/tags); the [/releases](https://github.com/hiero-hackers/hiero-streams-rs/releases) page stays empty unless someone remembers to create the release by hand.

This has already bitten us twice:

- `v0.2.0` was tagged and published on 2026-07-21 but never got a release entry (still missing).
- `v0.3.0` was tagged on 2026-08-02 and its release had to be created manually after the fact.

Consumers watching the repo for releases (or using the releases Atom feed) don't see new versions.

## Proposed fix

Add a small job to `release.yml` that creates the release automatically on tag push:

```yaml
github-release:
    name: Create GitHub Release
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')
    permissions:
        contents: write
    steps:
        - name: Create release
          env:
              GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          run: gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --title "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --generate-notes
```

Notes:

- `--generate-notes` builds the changelog from merged PRs since the previous tag, so no extra tooling is needed.
- The job needs `contents: write` (the workflow currently sets a top-level `contents: read`, so the elevated permission should be scoped to this job only, as above).
- The `if:` guard keeps `workflow_dispatch` (the manual fallback) from trying to create a release without a tag.
- Kept independent of the publish jobs (no `needs:`), matching the workflow's existing philosophy that each half re-runs and fails cleanly on its own. Alternatively it could `needs: [publish]` so a release only appears once the crate is actual

issues.body:
## 🆕🐥 First Timers Only

This issue is reserved for people who have never contributed to [Hedera](https://hedera.com) or any open source project in general.
We know that creating a pull request (PR) is a major barrier for new contributors.
The goal of this issue and all other issues labeled by [**'good first issue'**](https://github.com/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+org%3Ahashgraph+archived%3Afalse+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22+) is to help you make your first contribution to Hedera.

## 👾 Description of the issue

The Hedera SDK offers an example to demonstrate how to add and remove NFT allowances, which is a crucial process for controlling asset permissions. However, the complexity of the operations can make it difficult for developers to follow without a clear step-by-step breakdown.

## Solution 
This example in the Java SDK showcases the process of managing NFT allowances, including creating NFTs, approving and revoking permissions, and transferring tokens using the Hedera SDK. By following these steps, developers can implement allowance functionality efficiently. [NftAddRemoveAllowancesExamples.java](https://github.com/hashgraph/hedera-sdk-java/blob/main/examples/src/main/java/com/hedera/hashgraph/sdk/examples/NftAddRemoveAllowancesExample.java)

We need to provide that example for the RUST-SDK, too.

## Implementation
1. Set up the SDK client with the necessary operator account and key.
2. Create a unique NFT and retrieve the associated token ID.
3. Mint NFTs by attaching metadata to each unique token serial number.
4. Generate spender and receiver accounts with their respective keys.
5. Associate the spender and receiver accounts with the NFT token.
6. Grant allowance for specific NFT serials to the spender account.
7. Execute an NFT transfer using the approved allowance on behalf of the spender.
8. Revoke the allowance for specific NFT serial numbers.
9. Attempt another transfer after revocation to confirm the permission removal.

issues.title: Make the test timeout a configurable value
issues.body:
## 🆕🐥 First Timers Only

This issue is reserved for people who have never contributed to [Hedera](https://hedera.com) or any open source project in general.
We know that creating a pull request (PR) is a major barrier for new contributors.
The goal of this issue and all other issues labeled by [**'good first issue'**](https://github.com/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+org%3Ahashgraph+archived%3Afalse+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22+) is to help you make your first contribution to Hedera.

## 👾 Description of the issue

Currently, tests are hardcoded to timeout after 30 seconds. This should be made a configurable value.

### Proposed Solution

1. Add a `TEST_TIMEOUT` configuration value to the `.env.custom_node` and `.env.testnet` files that allows a user to control how quickly a test should timeout.
2. Make necessary code changes to pull in this value and set it for all test suites. This includes all `*.js` files under the `test/` directory. A `describe` block is used to demarcate the tests for a specific request type and within the `describe` block, there should be a `this.timeout(30000);` line or something to that effect. This is what specifies the timeout for tests. If no value is provided, a default value (30) should be used.
3. Verify the timeout. Follow the directions in the [README](https://github.com/hashgraph/hedera-sdk-tck/blob/main/README.md) to start an SDK server and configure the TCK to run with the [hedera-local-node](https://github.com/hashgraph/hedera-local-node) and run it. Change the `NODE_IP` value in your `.env` file to use a different port and set `TEST_TIMEOUT` to 2000. Run the TCK using `npm test run` and observe the tests failing after 2 seconds. You should be able to then change the value to 3000 to see the tests failing after 3 seconds.

If you have never contributed to an open source project at GitHub, the following step-by-step guide will introduce you to the workflow. More inf
